title: Intention is the act
hook: the Buddha calls intention itself kamma (AN 6.63)

segments.voice: Yesterday: samma kammanta, right action, a way of moving through the world with care. Your line: act with care.

Two people step on your foot on the same crowded train. One lurches when the brakes hit. The other looks right at you first, and then does it. Same foot. Same weight. Same bruise. And yet nobody would call them the same event. No philosophy class required; a small child on a playground already argues the difference between an accident and on purpose. The Buddha built a teaching on that instinct, and he put it in a single short sentence.
screen: `TWO PEOPLE, ONE FOOT.` → `A LURCH, OR A LOOK FIRST.` → `SAME BRUISE, DIFFERENT EVENT.`

segments.voice: The sentence is in the Numbered Discourses, in a sutta about seeing deeply into the teaching. The Buddha says, in plain terms: it is intention, monks, that I call kamma. Having intended, a person acts by body, by speech, and by mind. The Pali word for intention is cetanā: the mind's leaning toward something, its choosing. And kamma, karma in Sanskrit, simply means action, deed. Not fate. Not a cosmic scoreboard. A deed. So this is a definition, and a startling one. Which part of the train was the deed? Not the foot. The choosing. That's why the path spent days on right intention before it reached speech and action. The hand and the tongue are where an act shows up; the mind is where it's made. Two things follow. First, accidents aren't the heart of kamma. The lurch on the train isn't what the Buddha is pointing at, though carelessness can be a kind of choice too. Second, and harder: a deed can be done entirely inside. A long, deliberate grudge is a deed, even if no one ever sees it. The Dhammapada opens with the same idea, in Max Müller's words: "All that we are is the result of what we have thought." So if intention is the act, the place to practice is the half-second before the act. That small gap is where the choosing lives, and the choosing is the part that's yours.
screen: `CETANĀ: THE MIND'S CHOOSING.` · `KAMMA MEANS DEED, NOT FATE.` · `THE MIND IS WHERE IT'S MADE.` · `THE HALF-SECOND BEFORE.` · then, large: `INTENTION IS THE ACT.`

segments.voice: Rest with the breath and watch for the choosing: small impulses will arrive, to shift your weight, to scratch, to open your eyes, to check the time. Before you act on one, see whether you can catch the intention itself, the little lean toward doing. You may act on it or not; the point is to see it before the body moves.
Kamma. Action, deed; karma in Sanskrit. The Buddha defines it by intention, cetanā: having intended, one acts.
Your line: the half-second before the act. The hand is where it shows; the mind is where it's made. Catch you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often explain kamma by pointing to intention, and many practitioners make a habit of checking their motive before acting and of dedicating good deeds with a wholesome wish.

fork.setup: two people step on your foot. one lurches when the brakes hit; one looks at you first. by AN 6.63, which is kamma in the full sense?
fork.reveal: the Buddha calls intention kamma: the deed is the choosing, and the foot is only where it shows up.

original.note: Pali kamma (Sanskrit karma, कर्म): action, deed. AN 6.63 defines it as intention.

trapdoor: what you thought: karma is the universe paying you back.
what it means: kamma is a deed, and the Buddha says the deed is the intention.
what a scholar hears: AN 6.63 reads cetanāhaṃ, bhikkhave, kammaṃ vadāmi; some scholars read this as making kamma a matter of ethics and the mind rather than of ritual.

chat.says: Isn't karma basically fate, whatever's going to happen to you anyway?
options: Kamma means deed, and the Buddha said it's intention: the choosing is the act.
Yes, karma means your life was set in stone before you were born.
It's mostly about accidents, like stepping on someone's foot by mistake.
chat.meaning: In AN 6.63 the Buddha says: it is intention that I call kamma. Kamma means action, a deed, not fate.
